description:
Wesam Saad returns to questions raised by the previous study about present spiritual growth and future enjoyment of God. He explains his distinction between the believer’s renewed heart and the flesh in which sin remains, drawing on Ephesians, Ezekiel and Paul’s account of inner conflict. In his teaching, the new heart is righteous but must grow, while bodily glorification removes sin from the flesh. This does not excuse personal responsibility: believers must resist deception and follow the truth of Scripture. He contrasts the immediate rejection of sin with the continuing growth of love, patience and other fruit of the Spirit.

That distinction frames his argument that freedom from sorrow in the eternal state does not mean an identical capacity for joy in every believer. He urges listeners to take sanctification seriously now, while setting aside detailed questions about eternal rewards for later discussion. The session then examines sacrificial service as a means of growth. Using Ephesians 4:16, Saad describes Christ joining and gifting the church so that its members build one another up in love. Encouragement, teaching, counsel and practical help affect the whole body. Listeners are challenged to serve amid their own struggles, receive help from others and avoid limiting love to activities they regard as their particular gift.

questions.question: How does Saad distinguish the renewed heart from the flesh?
questions.answer: He teaches that God gives the believer a new heart, or new self, created in righteousness and holiness. Although that heart begins small and needs to grow, he describes sin as dwelling in the still unredeemed flesh. He uses this distinction to explain both Christian conflict and the continuing need for maturity.

questions.question: Does locating sin in the flesh remove the believer’s responsibility for wrongdoing?
questions.answer: No. Saad explicitly says believers remain responsible for sins committed in the flesh and must wage war against its desires. His distinction between heart and flesh is intended to explain the conflict, not to transfer accountability away from the person who sins.

questions.question: Why does the study emphasise truth rather than simply following the heart?
questions.answer: Saad describes the conflict largely as a battle between truth and deception. A believer may give way when deceived into thinking sin will satisfy more than Christ. He therefore urges listeners to follow Jesus through Scripture, rather than treating the heart’s immediate judgement as a sufficient guide.

questions.question: What does Saad mean when he describes glorification as subtraction?
questions.answer: In his explanation, bodily glorification removes sin from the flesh rather than replacing the person or instantly adding unlimited maturity to the heart. The believer remains an embodied human being. This distinction underpins his claim that spiritual growth in the present life has lasting significance.

questions.question: How do the commands to reject sin differ from the commands to grow in holiness?
questions.answer: Saad points to commands that require sin to be cut off completely and to commands that call for continuing growth in love, knowledge and the fruit of the Spirit. Resisting sin serves the positive goal of a growing heart. He warns that the struggle requires ongoing attention rather than a single past effort.

questions.question: How can capacities for joy differ without producing sadness in heaven?
questions.answer: Saad argues that believers can differ in their capacity to enjoy God while all are free from sinful misery, jealousy and discontent. He rejects the suggestion that contentment must depend on ignorance of those differences. He treats this as a reason to value present sanctification, while reserving detailed teaching about rewards for another occasion.

questions.question: What role does the church body play in the growth described by Ephesians 4:16?
questions.answer: Christ joins the members together and supplies their gifts, and the body grows as its members work in love. Saad applies this to mutual encouragement, teaching, mercy and other service. One person’s faithfulness or neglect affects others, so growth involves receiving and contributing within the church.

questions.question: Why should believers serve while they are still facing struggles of their own?
questions.answer: Saad describes people bringing their difficulties into a relationship of mutual help rather than waiting until every problem at home is resolved. Someone who needs counsel may still encourage another person who can counsel them. He also warns against using the limits of a particular gift as an excuse to withhold ordinary practical assistance.
